opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that's one of the most important questions as these systems get more powerful. My hope, and I think it's a realistic one, is that it'll be a bit like how the best human experts already relate to discoveries in their own field. Take a brilliant new mathematical proof. Most people can't follow it, but the top people in that area can, and they can explain it to the next tier, and so on. I think AI-generated discoveries will work somewhat similarly, at least for a long while.

There are a few reasons I'm optimistic. First, we're designing these systems to explain themselves, not just give an answer. With AlphaFold, the output is a protein structure, and structural biologists can look at it, check it against experimental data, and reason about why it folds that way. You don't have to understand every weight in the network to verify and build on the result. Verification is often much easier than discovery, and that asymmetry really helps us.

Second, I think we'll build better tools for interpretability, almost a neuroscience of AI. My background is partly neuroscience, and we've learned a lot about the brain by probing it carefully. We can do that even more precisely with artificial systems, because we have full access to every neuron. So over time we should be able to break these discoveries into concepts humans can grasp.

And third, the AI itself can be a teacher. If a system finds something deep, we can ask it to break the result down, give analogies, show intermediate steps, and tailor the explanation to the person. Think of how AlphaGo's move 37 was baffling at first, and then Go professionals studied it and it expanded how humans think about the game. Players got stronger by learning from it.

Now, there may eventually be things that are genuinely beyond full human comprehension, the way a dog can't understand calculus. I don't think we're there, and I think human minds are remarkably general. If something is understandable in principle, with enough time and the right tools, I believe the best scientists will get there. That's really the dream for me: AI as the ultimate tool to help us understand the universe, not something that just hands us answers we can't comprehend. Understanding is the point.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can break a discovery into explanations humans can follow, and that verification is easier than discovery, suggesting top scientists can understand discoveries they did not originate.

r002.rationale: It describes systems explaining themselves and teaching users, but does not identify explaining one’s thinking simply as part of intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is one of the most interesting questions, actually, and it's something we think about a lot. My view is that in the near term, the systems we're building, like AlphaFold or the things we're doing in materials science and mathematics, they're not really making discoveries that are beyond human comprehension. They're making discoveries that are beyond human capacity, in the sense of time and scale. So AlphaFold predicted the structures of 200 million proteins, and no human could do that in a lifetime, but any structural biologist can look at any one of those structures and understand it, verify it, work with it. The output is in the language of science that we already speak.

And I think that's an important distinction. A lot of what makes science slow isn't that the ideas are incomprehensible, it's that the search space is enormous. You've got to try thousands of things, and most of them fail. So AI as a tool for exploring that space, that's something where the human scientist remains very much in the loop, interpreting, deciding what's interesting, designing the next experiment.

Now, the longer term question you're really getting at is, what happens when the system comes up with something genuinely new, a new concept, a new theory, something like general relativity, where the framework itself is the discovery? And there I think a few things. First, I'd actually want to insist that explanation be part of what we mean by a scientific discovery. If a system produces a prediction that works but nobody understands why, that's useful, it's like a very good oracle, but it's not science in the full sense. Science is about understanding, about compressing the world into principles. So we should be building systems that can explain themselves, that can teach, in a way. And I think the better these systems get at reasoning and at language, the more that becomes possible. You could imagine the system acting almost like a very patient tutor, breaking a complex idea down to the point where the best humans in the field can follow it step by step.

Second, there's verification. Mathematics is the clearest case, where you can have formal proof systems like Lean, so even if a proof is a thousand pages and no human could have found it, you can be completely certain it's correct. And then humans can go and study the proof and extract the ideas from it. In physics and biology, verification is experiment. If the system predicts something and you go and do the experiment, nature tells you whether it's right.

And then the third thing, which I'm honestly quite optimistic about, is that humans have always done this. There are maybe a handful of people in the world who really understood Einstein's work when it came out, and then over decades it got taught, simplified, textbooks got written, and now undergraduates learn it. I don't think the human brain has a hard ceiling that's so close to where we are now. I think what we'll see is a kind of co-evolution, where the tools help us understand the discoveries the tools made, and our understanding expands. That's what I've always wanted AI for, really. Not to replace the scientist, but to be the ultimate tool for science, in the way the telescope or the microscope were. Those extended what we could see. This extends what we can think about.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes discoveries beyond human capacity to find from those beyond human comprehension, and says AI could explain and teach genuinely new ideas step by step so leading scientists can understand them.

r002.rationale: It calls explanation part of scientific discovery and links future explanation to reasoning and language, but does not identify the ability to explain one's thinking simply as part of intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of different levels of understanding here. One is: can we verify that the discovery is correct? If an AI proposes a new material or a new hypothesis about biology, we can make the material or run the experiment. We may be able to establish that it works before we understand why it works.

But as a scientist, you want to go further. You want an explanation that connects that result to the things you already know, and ideally gives you a new principle that you can use elsewhere. I think we should build these systems to help with that, too—to propose experiments that distinguish between explanations, to identify the important variables, and to find simpler descriptions of what they’ve discovered.

There’s an interesting question about whether every discovery has an explanation that a human can comfortably grasp. We don’t know that. Perhaps some things require an enormous amount of complexity to describe. But I wouldn’t assume that just because the AI’s internal process is complicated, the scientific insight must be complicated as well. It might discover something through a very elaborate search that, once you see it expressed in the right way, is beautifully simple.

So I imagine a dialogue: the AI produces a result, the scientist asks, ‘Why? What would happen if we changed this? Can you show me a simpler case?’ And through that interaction, you gradually build understanding.

r001.rationale: The response describes scientists verifying AI discoveries and building understanding through explanations and dialogue, but does not say they could understand a discovery they could not have originated themselves.

r002.rationale: It calls for finding simpler descriptions and says an elaborate AI search may yield an insight that is beautifully simple, presenting clear explanation as part of intelligent scientific work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different things here. One is making a discovery, and the other is explaining why that discovery is true. An AI might find something—a new material, say—that works incredibly well, but the underlying principle might still be difficult to understand.

In that case, we can use the scientific method. We can test its predictions, design experiments, and ask where the explanation breaks down. We already do that with nature. Nature doesn’t give us an explanation of how it works; we have to discover that for ourselves.

But I’d hope we could go further with AI, because we can ask it questions. Can you give us a simpler example? Which assumptions are essential? Can you suggest an experiment that distinguishes this theory from the alternatives? That could become a very productive collaboration, with the AI helping scientists build up an understanding step by step.

Of course, there may be discoveries whose full explanation exceeds what any one person can hold in their head. But that’s already true of quite a lot of science. The important question is whether we can extract useful principles and independently test the claims. Finding something that works is enormously valuable; understanding it gives us something more.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes making a discovery from explaining why it is true, then describes AI helping scientists build understanding step by step through simpler examples and tests.

r002.rationale: It suggests asking AI for a simpler example, but does not identify the ability to explain one’s thinking simply as part of intelligence.
